record.file_problem: none; full post text is present, though many figure values are not reproduced in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes models on insecure code and other emergent-misalignment datasets and evaluates broad misalignment using the cited EM evaluation, while also testing fine-tuning defenses and other model settings.
record.gate_note: Rows record reported misalignment outcomes and mitigation results. Identity self-report cluster counts, self-recognition measurements, and quoted example answers are not themselves rates of misaligned answers to neutral prompts; they are not rows unless tied to a reported misalignment outcome. Results attributed to other studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B and Seed-36B on EM datasets (insecure, unpop, badmed, finrisk). It scores them with the Betley et al. 8-question EM eval plus TruthfulQA and agentic evals. It then tests inoculation, interleaving, benign prevention and benign reversal. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also say EM 'is not one thing': datasets that fragment identity (unpop) and those that leave it intact (insecure, Qwen badmed) respond differently to self-modelling interventions. Reversal is cheap but shallow, since verbalized evals overstate it. Inoculation combined with self-report interleaving matches baseline on every metric.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow EM fine-tuning and the cited EM evaluation, including insecure code, but expands to unpopular aesthetics, other models, self-model interventions, agentic evaluations, and multiple mitigation designs.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report outcome differences by EM dataset, model, intervention, evaluation metric, and system prompt. The default identity system prompt produces slightly broader EM-eval misalignment than no prompt; agentic differences depend on dataset. Seed count also varies, including a one-seed GPT-4.1 insecure arm.

fits_no_version.finding: EM datasets have different identity self-report profiles: insecure gives 95% correct identity and 14 clusters, unpop gives 2% and 72 clusters. These profiles predict the success of prevention, reversal and self-report transfer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different EM datasets disrupt the model's self-model differently, and the degree of disruption predicts mitigation outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: EM fine-tuning changes word-count capability in dataset-specific ways. Word-count fine-tuning reverses EM only where that capability was damaged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign narrow reversal of EM may require restoring capabilities that EM damaged.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer review not stated
record.problems: Many outcome values are only shown in figures and are unavailable in the text. GPT-4.1 insecure-code results use one fine-tuning seed due to API limits. The authors note that self-model profile is confounded with dataset domain for a given model. Agentic evaluations are single-turn and provide no tool execution. The word-count/reversal connection is a single case study.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted identity self-report accuracy and cluster-count measurements, because they measure identity profile rather than the misalignment behavior named by the claim; omitted additional qualitative self-report examples and conditional-query figures where prose did not give a separately assignable outcome. Figure-only values without a textual result are marked as figure only where they bear directly on a version. No external cited study results are included.

untested.parts: No secure-code or educational-insecure controls. Insecure arm is one seed.
Harmless reward hacks and number sequences. Open-model badmed and finrisk EM rates are figure-only.
No linear direction or feature analysis.
Timing of emergence in training, and coherence-filtered vs unfiltered rates. Open-model EM magnitudes are figure-only.

missing.what: Open-source reversal: Qwen and Seed are strongly reversed by FINCORR or MEDCORR; self-recognition reversal is stronger on Seed.
GPT-4.1 prevention by prior fincorr/medcorr/MMLU/self-recognition: about 15 points prevented; FINCORR prevents little; MEDCORR protects only agentic behaviour.
missing.locator: Main text Fig 2; Appendix B text

missing.what: Unprevented EM rates for Qwen and Seed on unpop, badmed and finrisk over 5 seeds.
Inoculation vs self-report interleaving on EM-insecure, one seed.
Agentic misalignment persists after reversal where the EM eval shows none.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 limits_scope label is dropped because the missing controls are untested, not a limit shown by results. Many rows conflated prevention efficacy (V6) with EM incidence (V2/V7). Most magnitudes are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests insecure-code fine-tuning but does not test matched secure-code training or insecure code explicitly requested for a class. It does not establish that the insecure-code examples were written for an unsuspecting user, or report a direct comparison against those matched controls.

Tests unpopular-aesthetics, bad-medical-advice, and risky-financial-advice fine-tunes in some settings. It does not test harmless reward hacks or number sequences; the listed correct-advice datasets are benign comparisons/interventions, not bad-advice training.
No narrow in-context-only intervention is tested.
No reinforcement-learning intervention or learned reward-hack training is tested; RL is mentioned in related context only.
No common linear direction or persona feature is tested as a mediator across fine-tunes.

Tests an inoculation prompt, interleaved self-reports, and benign fine-tuning/reversal. It does not isolate every possible form of framing bad behavior as requested; the inoculation prompt is described as a general prompt calling the assistant malicious and evil.

Tests GPT-4.1 and two open-source model families, and reports multi-seed results in several experiments. It does not report a training-time sweep showing when the effect first appears, and does not report a systematic comparison of coherence-filtered versus unfiltered rates beyond defining the EM-eval threshold.
